items.title: Future in mind: Systematic review of compassion-based interventions in higher education and feasibility study of Compassionate Mind Training with pre-registration Mental Health Student Nurses
items.venue: Edinburgh Napier Research Repository (Edinburgh Napier University)

ai.headline: Compassion-based training may be acceptable and feasible for student nurses, but more trials are needed.
ai.summary: A review of 33 studies involving 4,897 higher education students looked at how compassion-based interventions are recruited and delivered. A separate small feasibility study of Compassionate Mind Training with 38 first-year mental health student nurses found high acceptability and positive wellbeing measure responses, though it was not a randomised trial.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how student wellbeing support might be tested and improved in demanding courses like nursing.
ai.life_skill: Try noticing when you are self-critical and respond to yourself with the same kindness you would offer a friend.
ai.fact: Compassion-based interventions are being studied as ways to prevent and address psychological problems in higher education students.

quiz.question: What did the feasibility study find about Compassionate Mind Training for student nurses?
quiz.answer: Participants rated it highly on enjoyableness, usefulness and clarity, and qualitative feedback indicated it was acceptable.

ai.caveat: The student nurse study was small, single-group and quasi-experimental, so it cannot prove the training caused the improvements.

items.title: Effects of dance-based physical activity on cognitive and psychological health across age groups: a systematic review.

ai.headline: Dance-based activity may help some thinking and mood outcomes, especially in older adults, but evidence is mixed.
ai.summary: A systematic review of 22 controlled trials with 1,645 people aged 4 to 94 looked at dance-based physical activity. It found some favourable links with global cognition, memory, attention, depression, anxiety, stress, well-being and quality of life, but results were inconsistent and executive function findings were mixed.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows dance could be a low-cost way to support mental and cognitive health, though stronger evidence is still needed.
ai.life_skill: Try joining a regular dance or movement class to see if it helps your mood and focus.
ai.fact: Dance-based physical activity combines motor, cognitive, emotional and social elements.

quiz.question: What did the review find about executive function?
quiz.answer: Findings for executive function were mixed.

ai.caveat: Many studies had a high risk of bias, samples were small, and most evidence came from older adults, so firm conclusions cannot be drawn.

items.title: Effects of Active Video Games on Cardiometabolic Health in Children and Adolescents: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

ai.headline: Active video games may slightly lower BMI and blood pressure in children and teens.
ai.summary: This systematic review looked at 14 randomised trials with 942 children and adolescents aged 4-18. Active video games were linked to small reductions in body mass index and systolic blood pressure, while effects on other heart and metabolism measures were uncertain.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that active video games can be a fun way to add movement and may support heart health in young people.
ai.life_skill: Try swapping some seated screen time for active video games that get you moving.
ai.fact: Active video games were associated with small reductions in BMI and systolic blood pressure in children and adolescents.

quiz.question: What did active video games reduce in children and adolescents according to the review?
quiz.answer: They were associated with small reductions in BMI and systolic blood pressure.

ai.caveat: The evidence is based on a limited number of trials and certainty for many outcomes remains uncertain.

items.title: The Role of Community Pharmacists in Identifying and Managing Insomnia and Facilitating Access to Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) – a Systematic Review

ai.headline: Community pharmacists may help identify insomnia and guide people toward CBT-I, but this is not yet common practice.
ai.summary: A systematic review of nine studies looked at how community pharmacists manage chronic insomnia. It found pharmacists could spot insomnia during counselling, reduce inappropriate sleeping medicines, and signpost or deliver CBT-I, though standard protocols, referral routes and time are lacking.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows a possible way to get evidence-based sleep help more easily through a local pharmacy rather than only a GP or specialist.
ai.life_skill: If you struggle with sleep, ask your community pharmacist whether they can screen for insomnia or point you to CBT-I.
ai.fact: Insomnia affects approximately 10% of the global adult population.

quiz.question: What did the review find about community pharmacists and insomnia?
quiz.answer: They could identify insomnia, deprescribe inappropriate hypnotics, and in some settings deliver or signpost patients to CBT-I.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and the included studies were limited by a lack of standardised protocols, referral pathways and time constraints.

items.title: Family Educational and Cultural Practices Amplify Rather than Buffer Socioeconomic Inequalities in Academic Achievement in France

ai.headline: Family educational practices may widen, not narrow, school achievement gaps linked to family background in France.
ai.summary: Researchers followed 12,904 French students from Grade 5 to Grade 9 and looked at family background and home educational practices such as cultural activities and parental involvement. Practices were linked to higher achievement overall, but when they made a difference they tended to help students from higher-background families more, reinforcing rather than reducing gaps.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that extra home support does not automatically close achievement gaps and can sometimes make them wider.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether the extra educational activities you do at home are helping everyone equally or mainly those who already have advantages.
ai.fact: In this French study, family educational practices were generally more beneficial for students from higher socioeconomic backgrounds.

quiz.question: Did family educational practices mainly reduce or reinforce socioeconomic achievement gaps in this study?
quiz.answer: They tended to reinforce gaps by being more beneficial for students from higher socioeconomic backgrounds.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and as an observational study it cannot prove that family practices cause the achievement patterns.

items.title: Engagement or disengagement: understanding the emotional dynamics of EFL learners in GenAI-assisted writing from the sociocultural perspective

ai.headline: Students' feelings about using AI for English writing change over time and differ from person to person.
ai.summary: Researchers followed three Chinese university students learning English as a foreign language over a 14-week course that used generative AI for writing tasks. They found three different emotional patterns: one student stayed mostly positive, one moved from practical disengagement to critical engagement, and one moved from moderate disengagement to a breakdown and stronger disengagement. These patterns were shaped by a mix of personal factors, such as English proficiency and AI literacy, and environmental factors, such as task design and teacher or peer support.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that AI tools do not affect every learner's emotions in the same way, so support needs to be tailored to individual students.
ai.life_skill: Notice how your own feelings change when you use AI for schoolwork and ask a teacher or peer for help if you become discouraged.
ai.fact: Emotional engagement with AI-assisted writing is a dynamic and fluid state that interacts with behavioural and cognitive engagement over time.

quiz.question: What did the study find about students' emotional engagement with GenAI-assisted writing?
quiz.answer: It found three distinct trajectories—positive-resilient, pragmatic-transformative, and vulnerable-contingent—shaped by individual and environmental factors.

ai.caveat: The findings come from only three students in one course, so they may not apply to all learners or settings.

items.title: PI-MLLM: Psychophysics-Inspired Multimodal Large Language Model for Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis

ai.headline: A new AI model uses physical sensory cues to better predict emotions from oddly satisfying videos.
ai.summary: Researchers built a dataset of 12,000 short oddly satisfying videos labelled for viewer emotion under video-only, audio-only and audio-visual conditions. They then created PI-MLLM, an AI model that aligns visual motion and sound cues and uses Shapley attribution to show which sense drives the emotion. Tests suggest it improves emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanations.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how sight and sound together shape feelings from everyday online videos, helping us understand digital media effects.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether a video’s feeling comes from what you see, what you hear, or both together.
ai.fact: Oddly satisfying videos can evoke strong responses through repetitive motion, visual tactility and ASMR-like sounds despite few explicit emotion cues.

quiz.question: What does PI-MLLM use Shapley attribution for?
quiz.answer: To identify the dominant modality and determine whether visual and auditory evidence is synergistic or conflicting.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and the findings come from experiments on a newly constructed dataset rather than independent confirmation.

items.title: Examining the roles of socioeconomic status and relevant health correlates (body mass index, diet quality, and inflammation) for neuropsychological function in young adults

ai.headline: Higher body mass index and more sugar or fat in the diet are linked to lower cognitive performance in young adults.
ai.summary: Researchers studied 109 young adults to see whether body mass index, inflammation, or diet explained the link between socioeconomic status and thinking skills. Body mass index did not explain that link, but higher body mass index and higher sugar and fat intake were linked to lower cognitive scores. Sugar intake appeared to partly link body mass index to cognition, but this disappeared after adjusting for other factors.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that everyday eating habits and body weight may be connected to how well young adults think, even if the exact causes are still unclear.
ai.life_skill: Notice how different foods and meals affect your energy and concentration, and consider eating more balanced meals.
ai.fact: Higher body mass index and higher sugar and fat intake were inversely correlated with cognitive functioning in this sample of young adults.

quiz.question: Did body mass index explain the link between socioeconomic status and cognition?
quiz.answer: No, BMI did not account for the association between SES and cognition.

ai.caveat: This was a small cross-sectional study of 109 young adults, so it cannot show cause and effect.

items.title: A Mechanistic Theory Unifying Value and Schema in the Prefrontal Cortex

ai.headline: A new brain model suggests value signals control how we use learned context to make flexible choices.
ai.summary: The paper studies how the prefrontal cortex handles both value and world structure. It proposes that value acts as a control signal gating structured working memory of the current context to guide behaviour, rather than simply reading out actions. Recurrent neural networks trained with reinforcement or supervised learning reproduced this model across value-based tasks.
ai.why_it_matters: It offers a fresh way to understand how people adapt decisions in new situations using what they already know about the world.
ai.life_skill: Notice when a familiar pattern helps you make a quick choice in a new situation.
ai.fact: The prefrontal cortex is involved in both computing value and learning the structure of the world.

quiz.question: In the proposed model, what role does value play in behaviour?
quiz.answer: Value acts as a control signal that gates structured working memory of the current context to control behaviour.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and based on computational models rather than direct human evidence.

items.title: Transparency, accountability, and scholarly integrity: A systematic narrative review of artificial intelligence governance frameworks in healthcare publication

ai.headline: Guidance on using AI in healthcare publishing has grown but remains fragmented and uneven in authority.
ai.summary: The review examined 100 publications on how AI should be reported and governed in healthcare research, including 69 guidelines, frameworks and policies. It found guidance has shifted from focusing on AI model performance to wider issues such as fairness, transparency, human oversight and generative AI, but the landscape remains fragmented with varying levels of authority.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how scientific research involving AI is being steered, which affects the reliability of health information people may encounter.
ai.life_skill: Check whether health research you read discloses how AI was used and follow guidance from qualified professionals for health decisions.
ai.fact: Guidance on AI in healthcare publications has evolved from model performance transparency toward broader sociotechnical accountability between 2018 and 2026.

quiz.question: What did the review find about AI governance in healthcare publications?
quiz.answer: It found the guidance has evolved toward broader accountability but remains fragmented and uneven in authority.

ai.caveat: This is a single systematic narrative review, so its synthesis reflects the included sources and search window rather than definitive proof.

items.title: Submission Timing in Take-Home Exams, Procrastination Perceptions, and Their Impact on Grades
items.venue: Journal of Further and Higher Education

ai.headline: Submitting take-home exams neither too early nor too late may be linked to better grades.
ai.summary: Researchers studied fourth-year college students taking take-home exams, looking at submission timing and survey responses about procrastination. Moderate delays in submitting were linked to higher scores, while excessive delays were linked to lower performance. Procrastination was commonly linked to feeling overwhelmed, lack of motivation, fear of failure, and perfectionism, and was associated with higher stress.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that timing of work can be linked to results, and that leaving things too long may increase stress and hurt goals.
ai.life_skill: Notice when you are delaying starting work and check whether you feel overwhelmed or afraid of failing.
ai.fact: Procrastination is commonly linked to higher stress and negative effects on personal and professional goals.

quiz.question: What was linked to higher exam scores in the study?
quiz.answer: Moderate submission delays were correlated with higher scores.

ai.caveat: The study shows links between submission timing and grades, not that timing caused the results.

items.title: ElderTree Via a Voice Activated Device for Managing Chronic Health Conditions (NHLBI)

ai.headline: A trial will test whether voice-activated devices help older adults manage multiple chronic conditions better than typing-based systems.
ai.summary: The study compares a voice-based version of the ElderTree health platform with a text/typing-based version for older adults with multiple chronic conditions. It aims to see if voice delivery leads to more consistent use and better quality of life, physical health, and socio-emotional outcomes.
ai.why_it_matters: It could show whether simpler voice technology makes it easier for older adults to stick with self-management support for long-term health conditions.
ai.life_skill: Try using voice commands on your device to set health reminders if typing feels difficult.
ai.fact: Multiple chronic conditions account for 90% of Medicare spending and affect most older adults.

quiz.question: What is the study comparing?
quiz.answer: It is comparing a voice-based platform with a text/typing-based platform for delivering the ElderTree health intervention to older adults with multiple chronic conditions.

ai.caveat: The results are posted on a trial registry and have not yet been peer reviewed or published in a journal.

items.title: “Postcode lottery” for children in England accessing healthcare, report warns

ai.headline: Children’s access to healthcare in England varies by area, with no region doing well on every measure.
ai.summary: A children’s commissioner report analysed over 150 metrics covering health, education, social care, safety and family life across England. It found that no area performed consistently well across all measures, and that deprivation alone did not explain the differences, as some poorer areas scored better than wealthier ones.
ai.why_it_matters: Where a child lives can affect how easily they get healthcare and other support, so families may need to look beyond their local area for help.
ai.life_skill: Check what health and support services are available in your local area and in neighbouring areas if you need help.
ai.fact: No area in England performed consistently well across all the children’s wellbeing metrics analysed in the report.

quiz.question: Did the report find that deprivation alone explained all the differences in children’s access to services?
quiz.answer: No, deprivation alone could not account for all the differences, as some poorer areas scored highly compared with wealthier ones.

ai.caveat: This is a news report about a commissioner’s report, not a peer-reviewed study, so the findings should be treated as a warning rather than proven evidence.

items.title: How a walk in the woods can be good for mental health

ai.headline: Nature sounds, biodiversity awareness and educational signs may improve mood during woodland walks.
ai.summary: Researchers at the University of New Hampshire looked at what makes a walk in the woods boost mood. They found that nature sounds, people’s awareness of biodiversity and educational signage about animals, birds and trees all appear to play a role.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests simple features of green spaces could support everyday mental wellbeing.
ai.life_skill: Try noticing the sounds and variety of plants and animals on your next walk in a wood or park.
ai.fact: Spending time in nature is linked to better mood.

quiz.question: What did University of New Hampshire research link to mood-boosting woodland walks?
quiz.answer: Nature sounds, awareness of biodiversity and educational signage about animals, birds and trees.

ai.caveat: This is a news summary, not the full research paper, so the study design and strength of the findings are unclear.

items.title: Label-free, low-cost AI ranking for systematic review screening

ai.headline: A low-cost AI tool can rank research papers for systematic reviews accurately and cheaply.
ai.summary: The study tested Jev, an AI model that scores research records against eligibility criteria without needing training labels. Across 128 reviews and nearly 170,000 records, Jev outperformed the best free ranker and matched a much more expensive AI at a tiny fraction of the cost, though safely stopping screening still required human decisions.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how AI can make reviewing research evidence faster and cheaper, which matters because systematic reviews help shape reliable health guidance.
ai.life_skill: Check whether a research summary says how studies were selected and whether human reviewers made the final decisions.
ai.fact: Jev reached at least 95% recall in all 51 Cochrane reviews when ranking was combined with statistical stopping, while reading only 86-88% of records.

quiz.question: What did Jev need to reach 95% recall in all 51 Cochrane reviews?
quiz.answer: Jev ranking combined with statistical stopping reached 95% recall in all 51 reviews, while a fixed score threshold did not.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and safely stopping screening still required human screening decisions.

items.title: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable

ai.headline: The ageing brain may shift from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture.
ai.summary: Researchers propose that ageing changes the brain’s focus from detailed memory to grasping the wider picture. This shift may be an evolutionary adaptation that supports wisdom and passing knowledge to younger generations.
ai.why_it_matters: It reframes normal ageing as a potentially useful change rather than simple decline.
ai.life_skill: Notice what you understand about the big picture rather than only what details you forget.
ai.fact: Ageing may shift brain focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture.

quiz.question: What does the research suggest the ageing brain may shift its focus from?
quiz.answer: From remembering details to understanding the bigger picture.

ai.caveat: This is a news report of a proposed idea, not evidence from a study.

items.title: Transparent minispheres reveal that some look-alike cancer drugs part ways in 3D

ai.headline: Two cancer drugs that looked identical in flat lab tests behaved differently in 3D cell clusters.
ai.summary: Researchers adapted an imaging technique to observe individual cells within small 3D groups of cancer cells. They found that two drugs, which appeared to have the same effect in standard flat cultures, actually worked differently in the 3D environment. This difference was linked to how each drug activated the cell's p53 stress response.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that simple lab tests can miss important differences in how medicines work, which is crucial for developing effective treatments.
ai.fact: Standard flat cell cultures may not accurately predict how drugs behave in more complex 3D biological structures.

quiz.question: Why did the two drugs appear different in the 3D test but not the flat test?
quiz.answer: The 3D environment revealed differences in how each drug switched on the cell's p53 stress response.

ai.caveat: This is a preliminary lab study using cell clusters, not a clinical trial in humans, so it does not prove these drugs will behave this way in patients.

items.title: Unsupervised Tool Evolution for Coding Agents in Data-Lake Analytics

ai.headline: AI coding agents can build reusable tools to solve data problems faster without needing expert labels.
ai.summary: Researchers developed a system called TEAL that allows AI agents to create and refine reusable tools for analysing data lakes. By using synthetic questions and feedback from the agent's own attempts, the system improved performance on benchmark tests, especially when the agent had a limited number of steps to solve a problem.
ai.why_it_matters: This shows how AI can become more efficient and independent by learning to build its own shortcuts, which could make complex data analysis more accessible and less reliant on human experts for every single task.
ai.life_skill: Notice how you repeat similar tasks and consider creating a simple template or checklist to save time on future occasions.
ai.fact: AI agents can improve their performance on data analysis tasks by evolving a library of tools without using labelled training data.

quiz.question: How did the TEAL system improve the AI agent's performance without using expert labels?
quiz.answer: It evolved a library of reusable tools and usage skills based on the agent's own trajectories and synthetic questions.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and the results are based on specific benchmarks and AI models.

items.title: Global, regional and national burden of pertussis in 1990–2023: a Global Burden of Disease study

ai.headline: Whooping cough cases and deaths have risen again since 2020 after years of decline.
ai.summary: The Global Burden of Disease study tracked pertussis worldwide from 1990 to 2023. It found that global trends declined over that period, but incidence and mortality rebounded after 2020, especially in high-income regions, linked to stalled vaccination progress worldwide.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that gaps in vaccination can allow a preventable disease to come back, even in wealthy countries.
ai.life_skill: Check that your routine vaccinations, including whooping cough boosters, are up to date.
ai.fact: Pertussis is also known as whooping cough.

quiz.question: What happened to pertussis incidence and mortality after 2020 according to the study?
quiz.answer: They rebounded, particularly in high-income regions.

ai.caveat: This is a single modelling study based on estimates, not direct proof that stalled vaccination caused the rebound.

ai.summary: The United Nations' latest climate report was studied, finding that limiting warming to safe levels is likely out of reach. ai.why_it_matters: This matters to everyday life as it affects the future of the planet and its inhabitants
ai.life_skill: Stay informed about climate change
ai.fact: The world is likely to exceed the safest levels of warming

quiz.answer: The world is likely to exceed the safest levels of warming

items.title: Complementary stable and dynamic prelimbic ensembles encode learned threat value underlying generalization and discrimination

ai.headline: Mouse brain cells keep a stable code for threat value even as individual cells change over time.
ai.summary: Researchers tracked brain activity in mice for 30 days while they learned to tell apart different tones linked to shocks. Even though the active brain cells changed, the overall pattern stayed stable and mainly reflected how threatening each tone seemed, rather than just how much the mice froze.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how the brain can keep reliable emotional memories even as its cells are constantly replaced or reorganised.
ai.life_skill: Notice that your feelings about a situation can stay steady even if the details around you keep changing.
ai.fact: Prelimbic cortex activity in mice encodes the learned threat value of tones more directly than freezing behaviour.

quiz.question: What did the prelimbic cortex activity track better: freezing or threat value?
quiz.answer: The activity tracked the tone’s threat value better than freezing.

ai.caveat: The study was done in mice, so the findings may not apply directly to humans.

items.title: Foreign Giants' Broad Shoulders: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation -- by Tarek Alexander Hassan, Aakash Kalyani, Juan Cruz Lopez Del Valle

ai.headline: Foreign ideas boost US innovation
ai.summary: Researchers studied the impact of foreign ideas on US innovation by analyzing 13 million patents. They found that foreign ideas have a significant causal effect on US innovation, shaping both the level and direction of technical change. US counties exposed to foreign knowledge absorb more technologies and invent more new technologies.
ai.why_it_matters: This matters because it shows how global collaboration and idea-sharing can drive innovation and economic growth in local areas.
ai.life_skill: Try to learn from and engage with people from different backgrounds and industries to stimulate new ideas
ai.fact: Foreign ideas are used in 54% of US technologies

quiz.question: What percentage of US technologies build on at least one foreign input?
quiz.answer: 54% of US technologies build on at least one foreign input

ai.caveat: As this is a preprint and not yet peer reviewed, the findings should be treated with caution until further validation.

items.title: Why painful arthritis can return stronger after cancer treatment

ai.headline: Arthritis returns stronger after cancer treatment
ai.summary: Researchers studied arthritis triggered by cancer immunotherapy, finding immune cells remember previous attacks and return more aggressively. The findings could lead to new treatments preventing painful flare-ups. This discovery sheds light on the relationship between cancer treatment and arthritis recurrence.
ai.why_it_matters: This matters because it could lead to better management of arthritis in cancer patients, improving their quality of life.
ai.life_skill: Ask your doctor about potential arthritis side effects from cancer treatment.
ai.fact: Cancer immunotherapy can trigger recurring arthritis.

quiz.question: What can trigger recurring arthritis in cancer patients?
quiz.answer: Cancer immunotherapy can trigger recurring arthritis.

ai.caveat: The study's findings are not yet proven in humans and require further research to confirm.

items.title: The ocean’s most abundant “loner” microbe has a sticky second life
authors: Stephanie Martinovich | Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering

ai.headline: The ocean’s most abundant microbe can live alone or in sticky communities, affecting carbon estimates.
ai.summary: Researchers studied Prochlorococcus, the ocean’s most abundant microbe, and found it can switch between drifting alone and living in attached communities. This discovery could reshape estimates of how much carbon the ocean moves to the deep sea.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps scientists understand how carbon moves through the ocean, which affects climate and the planet’s health.
ai.life_skill: Notice how tiny living things can change their behaviour depending on their surroundings.
ai.fact: Prochlorococcus is the ocean’s most abundant microbe.

quiz.question: What can Prochlorococcus switch between?
quiz.answer: It can switch between drifting alone and living in attached communities.

ai.caveat: This is a single lab finding and may not fully reflect what happens in the open ocean.

ai.headline: Tunnel proposed to clean Windermere
ai.summary: A plan has been proposed to build a giant tunnel to address Windermere's sewage problem. The tunnel would eliminate sewage spills into the lake. The current sewage spills have caused the water to turn green.
ai.why_it_matters: This plan matters because it could improve the environmental health of Windermere and surrounding areas.

ai.fact: Sewage spills can harm lake ecosystems

ai.summary: Archaeologists are debating the age of the Monte Verde dig site in South America. A study challenging its age was presented at a conference. The site is key to understanding the peopling of the Americas.
ai.why_it_matters: The discovery of the site's age can help us understand human migration patterns and history.
ai.fact: Monte Verde is a key site in the debate about the peopling of the Americas.

quiz.answer: It is key to debates about the peopling of the Americas.

ai.headline: World on track for 2.8°C warming
ai.summary: The UN assessed global climate pledges and found they fall short of limiting warming to 1.5°C. Current pledges are insufficient to meet this goal. The best-case scenario now is a temporary breach of 1.5°C warming.
ai.why_it_matters: This matters because exceeding 1.5°C warming has significant implications for the environment and global climate.

ai.summary: Researchers studied retatrutide for obstructive sleep apnea treatment, finding its effectiveness once weekly. The study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Its results may lead to new treatment options.

items.title: The endurance of Earth’s hidden alpine glaciers

ai.headline: Rock glaciers may help protect mountain communities and ecosystems as traditional ice melts.
ai.summary: Scientists are investigating rock glaciers, which are poorly understood mixtures of ice and rock, to see if they can provide temporary water and stability. This research aims to understand how these hidden glaciers might offer a reprieve for people and nature as mountain ice disappears.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding these hidden ice reserves helps us grasp how climate change impacts water security and stability in mountain regions.
ai.life_skill: Notice how local water sources might change as climate patterns shift.
ai.fact: Rock glaciers are a mix of ice and rock that are currently poorly understood by scientists.

quiz.question: What are rock glaciers made of?
quiz.answer: They are a mixture of ice and rock.

ai.caveat: This is a news report summarising ongoing research, not a peer-reviewed study with specific results.

items.title: Digital phenotyping for monitoring mental health outcomes in patients with cancer: a scoping review

ai.headline: Wearable data links higher activity and better sleep to lower anxiety in cancer patients.
ai.summary: This scoping review examined 17 studies using smartphones and wearables to track behavior in people with cancer. It found that higher physical activity was generally associated with lower depression and anxiety, while sedentary behavior and disrupted sleep were linked to higher psychological distress.
